passages.happening:
‘From inside the fish, Jonah prayed to the LORD his God’ (verse 1). He says that in his distress he called to the LORD, and the LORD answered. ‘From the belly of Sheol I called for help, and You heard my voice’ (verse 2).

God cast him into the deep, into the heart of the seas, and the waves swept over him (verse 3). He thought he had been banished from God's sight, and yet he would look again toward God's holy temple (verse 4). The waters closed around him, and seaweed wrapped around his head (verse 5). He went down to the roots of the mountains, and the earth barred him in. Then the prayer turns: “But You raised my life from the pit, O LORD my God!” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
In Israel's world the sea and the deep were pictures of chaos and death. Sheol was the realm of the dead, imagined beneath the earth, and the pit is another name for it. To sink into the sea was, in the language of poetry, to go down toward Sheol. The roots of the mountains reflect the old picture of mountains founded in the waters beneath the earth, and the earth barring him in pictures the underworld as a city whose gates close behind the dead.

The chapter is a story frame around a poem, and the poem follows the shape of a psalm of thanks: a summary of rescue, a description of the distress, the turn, and a vow of praise. It moves down and then up: down into the deep, then up as Jonah's prayer rises to God's temple and his life is raised from the pit. Almost every line echoes the psalms.

Jonah was a prophet from the north, but the psalms he echoes look toward the temple in Jerusalem, and holy temple can also mean God's dwelling in heaven. Both may be meant.
passages.later: A psalm begins almost the same way: ‘In my distress I cried to the LORD, and He answered me’ (Psalm 120:1). Another says, ‘all Your breakers and waves have rolled over me’ (Psalm 42:7).
passages.hard:
Could a man really survive three days inside a fish?

Readers differ, often in line with their view of what kind of book Jonah is, and this site takes no side. Those who read Jonah as history take it as a miracle, noting that the text says God appointed the fish and that Jesus spoke of it beside other events of history. Stories are sometimes told of sailors surviving inside a whale, but they are poorly documented, and they are not needed for a miracle. Those who read Jonah as a teaching story or parable see the fish as part of a deliberately extraordinary tale meant to teach, not a claim to be tested by science. Many in both groups note that three days and three nights can be an idiom for a period touching three days, which is how Jesus' own burial is counted.

On any reading, the story tells that God rescued a disobedient prophet from death. The book's real question is not the fish but whether Jonah, and the reader, will share God's mercy.
passages.asks: Jonah prayed from the bottom of the sea, and God heard. Ask whether you have believed you were too far down for God to hear you. And ask what you have said to God from your own deep places.

passages.happening:
‘As my life was fading away, I remembered the LORD. My prayer went up to You, to Your holy temple’ (verse 7). ‘Those who cling to worthless idols forsake His loving devotion’ (verse 8).

Jonah vows to offer thanks and sacrifice, and to fulfill what he has promised. The prayer ends, “Salvation is from the LORD!” (verse 9). ‘And the LORD commanded the fish, and it vomited Jonah onto dry land’ (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
A psalm of thanks was sung in the temple after a rescue, often with a thank offering and the keeping of a vow made in distress. Jonah's closing promise follows that pattern, and it echoes the sailors, who also offered sacrifice and made vows in chapter 1. The word for worthless idols means emptiness or vapor, a word the psalms use for false gods.

Scholars debate whether the psalm was written by the author of the story, taken from an existing psalm, or added later. Some note that its thankful, devout tone is different from the Jonah of chapters 1 and 4. Others argue that the contrast is deliberate, balancing this prayer with Jonah's very different prayer in 4:2-3.

The ending is abrupt and earthy. After the high confession that salvation is from the LORD, the fish vomits Jonah onto dry land. Some interpreters hear irony in it.
passages.later: A psalm also says, ‘I hate those who cling to worthless idols’ (Psalm 31:6). Jesus said that no sign would be given ‘except the sign of the prophet Jonah’ (Matthew 12:39).
passages.asks: Jonah says that those who cling to empty idols forsake God's loving devotion. Ask what you have been clinging to that cannot hold you. And Jonah made promises in the deep. Ask whether you have kept the ones you made in yours.
